candidate_phrase: Leaving social media does not mean leaving online life
provisional_trend: People appear to be moving toward selective exit, quiet use, and private or professional channels rather than complete disconnection.
repetition_rule: At least one public item on each of four platforms, with both complete-exit and selective-retention language present.
supporting_signal: Accounts describe deleting or limiting some platforms while retaining LinkedIn, Reddit, YouTube, or valued relationships; replies repeatedly debate whether substitution counts as quitting.
counter_signal: The sample may reflect a self-improvement and digital-minimalism subculture; a few visible accounts cannot show a broad shift in behavior.
research_check: After the candidate was frozen, the atlas research found reversible non-use, social pressure, substitution, and a separate U.S. deactivation experiment. It supports the selective-exit mechanism but does not establish a broad new trend or durable exit rate.
next_test: Collect a second dated wave, sample non-influencer accounts, and compare public claims with measured platform-use and non-use data.
limits: Two X items depend on limited direct or mirrored visibility

candidate_phrase: AI companion continuity and exit rights are becoming part of the relationship
provisional_trend: Public discussion increasingly treats memory, updates, deletion, privacy, and product shutdown as relationship events rather than ordinary software changes.
repetition_rule: At least three platforms must independently mention continuity, privacy, control, or the cost of losing access; current wave has four.
supporting_signal: Users and professional discussions repeatedly mention memory, deletion, disclosure, dependence, and sudden changes alongside emotional support.
counter_signal: Some public discussion treats AI companionship as temporary role-play or a useful tool, and some research relays report that companion use is rare in general-purpose chatbot data.
research_check: After the candidate was frozen, the U.S. survey and farewell experiments supported emotional connection, disclosure, short-run exit friction, and perceived loss. They do not establish durable relationships, general product shutdown effects, or widespread dependence.
next_test: Separate dedicated companion users from ordinary chatbot users and look for dated evidence of continuity loss, switching, or offline relationship change.
limits: X trending summaries are not direct post samples
Candidate may describe product concern rather than a social trend

candidate_phrase: AI layoffs are being discussed as a demand and legitimacy problem, not only an employment problem
provisional_trend: Public discussion links AI-driven job cuts to who can still buy products, whether firms are telling the truth about automation, and whether productivity gains are shared.
repetition_rule: The demand, legitimacy, or AI-washing frame must appear in at least two platforms and include one counter-frame about new work or efficiency.
supporting_signal: Public items connect layoffs to consumer demand, firm explanations, younger-worker opportunity, and the split between automation and complementarity.
counter_signal: The sample includes research relays and X summaries, not a broad worker sample; layoffs may also reflect over-hiring, finance, or ordinary restructuring.
research_check: After the candidate was frozen, the research supported uneven AI adoption, weaker early-career hiring and entry earnings in highly exposed groups, and a gap between productivity and worker control. It does not establish that AI caused all layoffs, that firms are AI-washing, or that demand effects are widespread.
next_test: Compare company-stated AI reasons with verified layoffs, hiring, output, wages, and local demand without assuming the stated reason is causal.
limits: Only three source records in the first wave
X item is an X-generated trend summary
Public debate may amplify extreme cases
